summary: Specifies how to put audio from the ITU-T G.711.1 codec into RTP packets, and registers two media types. This is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to pack sound recorded in one particular audio format into small packages for sending over the Internet, so a receiver can unpack and play it.

questions: how to send g.711.1 audio over rtp
how is g.711.1 carried in rtp
what is the g.711.1 mode-set parameter
subtitle: How to put wideband G.711.1 voice into RTP packets, with a one-byte header that says which quality mode follows.

tldr.problem: G.711.1 is a wideband extension of the G.711 voice codec, and it needs a standard way to be carried in RTP packets for Voice over IP.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet starts with a 1-octet payload header holding a 3-bit mode index, followed by one or more 5-ms frames of that mode. Two new media types, audio/PCMA-WB and audio/PCMU-WB, carry an optional mode-set parameter for negotiation.
tldr.outcome: G.711.1 packets can be turned into plain G.711 by stripping the upper layers, so deployments can mix old and new endpoints.

today: RFC 5391 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It registered the audio/PCMA-WB and audio/PCMU-WB media types.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
ITU-T Recommendation G.711.1 is an embedded wideband extension of the G.711 audio codec. RFC 5391 specifies how G.711.1 encoded audio is packetized into the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP).

The document also registers two media types. It uses the RFC 2119 key words, so MUST and SHOULD carry their usual force.
sections.plainLanguage: A new, better-sounding kind of phone audio needs a standard way to ride inside Internet packets. This RFC is that recipe.

sections.title: The G.711.1 Codec: Layers and Modes
sections.content:
G.711.1 operates at 64, 80 and 96 kbps. At 64 kbps it is fully interoperable with G.711, which is why an efficient deployment in existing G.711-based VoIP infrastructures is foreseen. The codec works on 5-ms frames and its default sampling rate is 16 kHz. Input and output at 8 kHz are also supported for narrowband modes.

The encoder produces an embedded bitstream in three layers: L0 (G.711 compatible, 64 kbps), L1 (narrowband enhancement, 16 kbps) and L2 (wideband enhancement, 16 kbps). The bitstream can be truncated by the decoder or by any component of the communication system to adjust the bit rate on the fly.

Combining layers gives four modes: R1 (L0, narrowband, 64 kbps), R2a (L0 and L1, narrowband, 80 kbps), R2b (L0 and L2, wideband, 80 kbps) and R3 (all three layers, wideband, 96 kbps).
sections.plainLanguage: The sound comes in layers, like a sandwich. The bottom layer is the basic old-style voice, and extra layers add clearer sound on top. You can eat the sandwich with fewer layers if you need to.

sections.title: RTP Header Usage
sections.content:
The RTP header follows RFC 3550. G.711.1 defines nothing specific for silence suppression (DTX), so codec-independent mechanisms such as the comfort-noise format of RFC 3389 may be used. For applications that send no packets or occasional comfort-noise packets during silence, the first packet of a talkspurt SHOULD have the marker bit set to one. Applications without silence suppression MUST set it to zero.

The payload type assignment is outside the scope of this document; the RTP profile is expected to assign one or make it dynamic.

The timestamp clock runs at 16 kHz. Even if the encoder input or decoder output is configured at 8 kHz, a 16-kHz RTP clock rate MUST always be used. One frame lasts 5 ms, which is 80 samples at 16 kHz, so the timestamp increases by 80 for each consecutive frame.
sections.plainLanguage: The packet's label has a clock that always ticks at the same fast speed, even if the recording was made more slowly. Each 5-ms slice of sound moves the clock forward by 80 ticks.

sections.title: The Payload Format
sections.content:
The payload is a payload header of 1 octet, followed by one or more consecutive G.711.1 frames of the same mode. The mode may change between packets, but not within a packet.

The five most significant bits of the header are reserved: they MUST be set to zero and MUST be ignored by receivers. The remaining 3 bits are the Mode Index (MI). MI 1 means R1 with 40-octet frames, 2 means R2a with 50 octets, 3 means R2b with 50 octets and 4 means R3 with 60 octets. Other MI values are reserved and MUST NOT be used; payloads with an undefined MI value MUST be discarded, as MUST payloads whose MI is outside a mode-set restricted by signaling.

Frames are packed oldest first. Within a frame the layers are always in the same order: L0 then L1 for R2a, L0 then L2 for R2b, and L0, L1, L2 for R3. The receiver finds the frame count by dividing the audio data size by the frame size for the mode. Only full frames count, and any remainder bytes MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package starts with a sticker saying which quality level is inside. After that come the sound slices, oldest first, each the same size. Any crumbs left over at the end get thrown away.

sections.title: Media Types and SDP Negotiation
sections.content:
Both A-law and mu-law G.711 can form the core layer, and the two are not interoperable. So the RFC registers audio/PCMA-WB (A-law core) and audio/PCMU-WB (mu-law core), with identical optional parameters: mode-set, ptime and maxptime. The mode-set is a comma-separated list drawn from 1, 2, 3, 4, in order of preference, and frames in other modes MUST NOT be sent. If it is absent, all modes are allowed. The ptime and maxptime values should be multiples of 5 ms.

In SDP, the subtype goes in a=rtpmap with a clock rate that MUST be 16000, and mode-set is copied into a=fmtp.

In offer/answer (RFC 3264), the offerer SHOULD also offer plain PCMA or PCMU, with G.711.1 preferred. The mode-set applies in both directions. If the offer has one, the answerer MUST return the same set or a subset of it, and MAY change the order. The offerer MUST NOT send a mode the answerer removed. Unknown parameters in an offer MUST be ignored and left out of the answer. For declarative SDP, nothing specific is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a call, both sides agree which quality levels they will use, like two friends agreeing which language to speak. If one friend only knows the old language, the call still works.

sections.title: Working with Plain G.711
sections.content: The L0 layer of G.711.1 is fully interoperable with G.711 and is embedded in every G.711.1 mode. A gateway can therefore take the audio data of a packet and strip the upper layers (L1 and/or L2), with no need to decode and re-encode the audio. If a packet holds several frames, joining the L0 layers of each frame forms a G.711-compatible payload.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the basic layer is the same as the old format, a helper in the middle can just peel off the extra layers and pass the plain voice along.

sections.title: Congestion Control and Packing Frames
sections.content:
Congestion control for RTP SHALL be used in accordance with RFC 3550 and any appropriate profile such as RFC 3551. The embedded design helps: a lower bit rate mode can be selected when needed, but only if several modes were negotiated (no mode-set, or a mode-set with at least two modes).

The number of frames per packet also affects bandwidth because of header overhead. Packing more frames reduces the packet count and overhead, at the cost of more delay and less robustness to errors.
sections.plainLanguage: If the road is jammed, the sender can switch to a smaller layer stack. Putting many slices in one box saves boxes, but you wait longer to fill it and a lost box loses more.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets are subject to the general security considerations of RFC 3550 and the profile in use. The main issues are confidentiality, integrity protection and authentication of the audio itself. The payload format has no built-in security mechanisms, but suitable external ones, such as SRTP (RFC 3711), MAY be used.

The format and the encoding do not show significant non-uniformity in receiver computational load, so they are unlikely to pose a denial-of-service threat from pathological datagrams, and they contain no active content such as scripts.
sections.plainLanguage: The package has no lock of its own, so if the call is private you need to add a lock from outside. Opening the package is not risky, though, because it holds only sound.
